name: Battle of Agincourt

sides.name: Kingdom of England
sides.commander: Henry V, Edward of Norwich (vanguard), Thomas Erpingham (archers), Humphrey of Gloucester
sides.strength: About 6,000 to 9,000 troops, around five sixths of them longbowmen
sides.casualties: Around 400 killed, including Edward of Norwich and several knights

sides.name: Kingdom of France
sides.commander: Charles d'Albret (constable), Jean le Maingre (marshal Boucicaut), Charles I d'Orléans, Jean I, Duke of Bourbon
sides.strength: About 14,000 to 25,000 troops, dominated by men-at-arms on foot and horse
sides.casualties: Around 6,000 killed including the constable, three dukes, and most of the high French nobility; 1,500 captured

summary: Henry V's exhausted army, three weeks marching from Harfleur to Calais, found the French host blocking the road at a narrow defile between the woods of Agincourt and Tramecourt. The English drew up with their longbowmen on the wings behind hammered stakes. The French men-at-arms attacked across a freshly ploughed and rain-sodden field, were funnelled into a killing ground by the woodlines, and were shot down by the arrowstorm before they could close. Henry ordered the killing of most of the noble prisoners during a second French rush, fearing a renewed attack from the rear. By evening the cream of the French aristocracy lay dead in the mud.
significance: Agincourt entered English national myth at Shakespeare's hand and remains the most cited demonstration of the late-medieval English longbow against armoured cavalry. The political consequence was the Treaty of Troyes (1420), which made Henry V heir to the French throne and produced the dual monarchy under his infant son. The military lesson, the value of dismounted men-at-arms supported by missile troops on chosen ground, foreshadowed the end of mounted feudal warfare in western Europe.
